subject: compound-interest
title: Compounding: The Arithmetic and the Leaks
summary: Rule-of-72 precision, fee drag, and teaching it at the kitchen table.

cards.title: The 1% that isn't small
cards.text: A 1% annual fee sounds like a rounding error. Over 30 years at a 7% gross return, it takes roughly a quarter of the ending value. Why is the intuition so far off?

cards.title: Rule of 72, checked
cards.text: Exact doubling time is ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + r). At 9%: 0.693 ÷ 0.0862 ≈ 8.04 years, versus 72 ÷ 9 = 8. With continuous compounding the constant is 69.3. 72 is a convenient, slightly high stand-in that divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 12.

cards.title: Fee drag
cards.text: $1 at 7% for 30 years grows to 1.07³⁰ ≈ 7.61. At 6% (7% minus a 1% fee), 1.06³⁰ ≈ 5.74. The fee costs about 25% of terminal wealth, not 1%, because it compounds against you every year.
cards.example: Same logic for taxes on turnover and for cash drag: small rate gaps, huge terminal gaps.

cards.title: Back-loaded payoffs
cards.text: $100 at 5% gains about $63 in years 1 to 10 and about $176 in years 11 to 25. Most dollar gains arrive late, so interruptions (withdrawals, panic selling, starting late) cost most at the end, where they are least visible in advance.

cards.title: Teaching it
cards.text: Investor.gov's classroom version: skip a $2 slice a day, save $730, invest at 5%. That is $931.69 after 5 years and $3,155.02 after 30. Kids feel the sacrifice now and see the payoff later, which is the whole psychological problem in one example.
cards.example: Investor.gov's free calculator lets the girls test their own numbers.

cards.question: Where else in your work does a small recurring rate (churn, defect rate, fee, error rate) compound into a large terminal effect that people underweight?
nudges: Translate one "small" annual rate into a 10-year multiplier.
Which of these leaks is actually controllable?

questions.q: At a 7% gross return, a 1% annual fee over 30 years reduces terminal wealth by about…

options.why: The fee compounds every year, so the loss is far larger.
Too large for a 1-point gap over 30 years.

questions.q: Exact doubling time at 9% annual compounding is about…

options.why: ln 2 ÷ ln 1.09 ≈ 8.04; the Rule of 72 says 8.
That would be the Rule of 72 at 10%.
That is closer to the continuous-compounding constant at 10%.

questions.q: Why is the constant 69.3 for continuous compounding?

options.why: Doubling time = ln 2 ÷ r with continuous compounding.
Inflation is not part of the derivation.
Daily compounding is close to continuous, but 69.3 comes from ln 2.
